h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in Upstate New York
intro:
Upstate New York is full of houses built to last a century, and most of them have now lasted that long. From the Buffalo double to the Albany brick rowhouse, the inventory investors buy in Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse and Albany is old, solidly built and in need of the same things: roofs that can carry heavy snow, heating that will not quit in January, wiring and plumbing from this century and lead-safe paint work on almost every surface. Each city also has its own rental rules, and the state's long judicial foreclosure process leaves many bank-owned houses vacant for a long time.

Genstone Construction renovates investment properties across upstate New York for individual investors, funds, lenders, servicers and Government-Sponsored Enterprises. We manage every project from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters and coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in each market. Every job begins with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, continues with a detailed scope and draw schedule, and is run by one field manager. You pay nothing upfront, and draws are tied to completed work.

sections.body:
The cities Genstone serves in New York grew during the same industrial century, so their housing shares a family resemblance with important local differences.

Buffalo is the city of the two-family double: a narrow, two-and-a-half story frame house with a flat on each floor, built mostly between the 1890s and the 1920s on stone foundations. Rochester has more detached single-family houses, block after block of colonials, foursquares and bungalows from the streetcar era, along with stacked two-families. Syracuse mixes frame two-families on the Northside and Westside with larger houses near the university and postwar singles in Eastwood, much of it on hilly lots. Albany's core is the nineteenth century brick rowhouse, with shared party walls and low-slope roofs, while its western neighborhoods add frame two-families and detached colonials.

Across all four, the renovation issues repeat. Lead paint is assumed because nearly everything predates 1978. Knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, cast-iron drains and old boilers with asbestos pipe wrap are common. Stone, brick and block foundations let water in on clay soils, and decades of snow have worn out roofs, porches and gutters. The structure is usually sound. The systems and envelope usually are not.

Each upstate city supports a slightly different mix of strategies.

In Buffalo, doubles in neighborhoods such as Black Rock, Riverside, South Buffalo and the West Side are the backbone of BRRRR and buy-and-hold portfolios, while Parkside, North Buffalo and the Elmwood Village support single-family and two-family flips. The East Side offers the lowest entry prices and the widest condition spread.

Rochester has been a competitive single-family rental market, with flips concentrated in the 19th Ward, Highland Park, the South Wedge and North Winton Village. Its rental certificate of occupancy and lead inspection rules make compliance a central part of every rental scope.

Syracuse divides between student rentals around the university, owner-occupant demand in Eastwood, Strathmore and Sedgwick, and low-cost two-families and land bank properties on the Northside, Near Westside and South Side. The Interstate 81 project and Micron's planned campus in Clay have drawn attention, though values should rest on current sales.

Albany's stable government and medical employment support rentals in Pine Hills and Park South, rowhouse restorations in Center Square and Hudson/Park, and family flips in Helderberg and Whitehall. Across the state, land banks created under New York's land bank law offer vacant properties to buyers who commit to renovating them.

sections.h2: Permits and licensing in New York
sections.body:
Outside New York City, construction is governed by the New York State Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code, usually called the Uniform Code, along with the state energy code. Each city, town and village enforces it through its own building department, so a project in Buffalo goes through the Department of Permit and Inspection Services, one in Syracuse through the Central Permit Office and one in Albany through the Department of Buildings and Regulatory Compliance.

New York does not issue a statewide general contractor license. Licensing for electricians, plumbers and, in some counties, home improvement contractors is handled locally, so trades must hold whatever licenses the specific city or county requires. Electrical inspections upstate are commonly performed by approved third-party inspection agencies.

Rental regulation is also local. Buffalo and Syracuse maintain rental registries, Rochester requires a rental certificate of occupancy that includes lead checks, and Albany requires a residential occupancy permit. Historic districts in all four cities add design review for exterior work.

For servicers, New York's zombie property law requires maintenance and state registry reporting for vacant and abandoned houses during foreclosure. Lead-safe work under the EPA renovation rule applies to pre-1978 housing everywhere. Genstone handles permits, inspections and lien waivers in each market.

Upstate New York's weather shapes both what goes into a scope and when it can happen. Lake-effect snow from Lake Erie and Lake Ontario can bury Buffalo and Syracuse in heavy, wet snow, and Rochester gets its share as well. Albany sees less lake-effect but deals with nor'easters, ice storms and long cold stretches. Everywhere, deep winter frost and repeated freeze-thaw cycles in fall and spring are hard on masonry, mortar, concrete steps and porches.

Those conditions put the roof, the attic and the heating system at the top of most scopes. Ice dams are common where attics lose heat, so a reroof should include ice and water barrier at the eaves, and the real fix often involves air sealing and insulation. Footings for porches and decks must sit below frost depth.

Scheduling follows the seasons. Roofing, siding, painting, masonry and concrete are best planned from late spring to early fall. Interior work, including framing, mechanicals, insulation and finishes, runs through winter once a house is enclosed and heated. Vacant houses face a serious risk of frozen and burst pipes from November onward, so winterization and monitoring protect a project between purchase and start. Spring thaw is the honest time to see how water moves around a foundation.

faqs.q: Which New York cities does Genstone serve?
faqs.a: In New York, we currently serve Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse and Albany, along with their surrounding towns. Each city page covers its housing stock, common issues, permits and climate, plus specific guidance for fix-and-flip, BRRRR, rental, small multifamily, FHA 203(k) and REO projects. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in each market and manage every project from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters, with one field manager assigned from start to finish.

faqs.q: Do upstate New York rentals need special inspections?
faqs.a: It depends on the city. Rochester requires a rental certificate of occupancy with lead checks, Albany requires a residential occupancy permit, and Buffalo and Syracuse maintain rental registries with inspections. Requirements change, so owners should confirm them with each city. Because nearly all upstate rental housing predates 1978, lead hazards are a common focus, and our rental scopes address peeling paint, friction surfaces like old windows and the safety items inspectors check most often.

faqs.q: How does New York's foreclosure process affect REO renovations?
faqs.a: New York forecloses through the courts, and the process can be slow, so many bank-owned houses have been vacant for a long time before the servicer takes possession. The state's zombie property law requires servicers to maintain vacant and abandoned houses during foreclosure and report them to a state registry. In practice, that means preservation often starts early, and REO scopes frequently include freeze damage, roof leaks, mold and open code violations.
